story_v1.post:
“What were you feeling when you decided to switch?”

That’s the question I’d use for a brand-switching study.

I want to hear what happened around the decision and what the person tried before it. I’d keep their exact words beside the campaign brief so the team can check what the customer actually said.

The slides show how I’d set up that study. The question studio has examples you can adapt.

slides.title: What made your customer switch?
slides.body: Ask them to take you back to the decision. Their account of that day gives you a place to start the research.

slides.title: Choose the event before the question.
slides.body: For a switching study, define the change you want to understand. It could be a move between brands in your category. Ask about a recent decision that the person can describe, and record when it happened with the answer.
slides.note: Interview question: “What were you feeling when you decided to switch?”

slides.title: Recruit people who made that change.
slides.body: Check that each participant used an alternative before choosing the new brand. Ask which products they used and when they changed. Keep those answers with the response so your team knows whose experience it is reading.

slides.title: Let people answer in their own words.
slides.body: Send the question with the event clearly named. Give participants space to describe what they felt and what was happening. Keep their responses intact in the results file so the campaign team can read each person’s account in context.

slides.title: Keep the quote beside its context.
slides.body: Save the exact phrase with the event it describes. Look across the responses for repeated reasons and exceptions. If one person mentions a problem, keep that observation at the level the evidence supports when sharing it with the campaign team.
slides.note: Working file: quote → event → possible message → evidence needed.

slides.title: Write the question around their decision.
slides.body: Agree on what the campaign team needs to learn before collecting responses. The question studio includes examples of events and participant criteria. You can use it to work out who belongs in the study and what you’ll ask them.

story_v1.plainPost:
Our deliverable is the results file.

The person reading it should be able to see what we asked and the words people used in reply.

If a customer describes the day they switched brands, keep that account together. The campaign team needs the context around a phrase before deciding to use it.

I’d put the original response beside any proposed copy. You can then check whether the draft still says what the person meant, and ask permission before publishing their words.
story_v1.magnetPost:
“What were you feeling when it happened?”

Before you send that question, decide which event you want people to describe.

For a brand-switching study, that could be the purchase that replaced their previous brand. Your panel needs to have made that change.

I put together a question studio with example events, participant criteria and the wording to send. You can start with one of the examples and copy the question.

story_v1.next: When does the team need the findings? I can help work out who to ask and whether a pilot would fit the launch.
story_v1.subject: Keep the response beside the campaign draft
story_v1.email:
Hi Alex,

When a customer phrase makes it into a campaign draft, keep the original response beside it.

Did the person describe why they switched, or a problem they ran into afterwards? Does your draft still mean what they said?

Save the event and the question with the quote. The next person reviewing the copy can then check it against the response.

Andrew
